text:
The dynamics between Jay Gatsby and Daisy Buchanan serve as the central vehicle for F. Scott Fitzgerald’s critique of the American Dream and the illusion of social mobility. Gatsby’s obsession with Daisy is not merely romantic; it is symbolic. He views her as the ultimate prize of his self-made success, a tangible representation of the status and wealth he believes he has earned. However, Daisy herself is shallow, careless, and bound by the rigid class structures of old money. This disconnect highlights the theme of illusion versus reality: Gatsby constructs an idealized version of Daisy that does not exist, just as he constructs an idealized version of the American Dream that ignores the entrenched privilege of the East Egg elite.

The tragedy arises because Gatsby’s pursuit is directed at a symbol rather than a person. His relentless effort to rewrite the past and win Daisy back underscores the futility of trying to transcend social barriers through material accumulation alone. The corruption of the American Dream is evident in how Gatsby’s noble aspiration for self-improvement is twisted into criminality and moral decay, all in service of a hollow goal. Ultimately, the failure of their relationship demonstrates that the American Dream, when reduced to materialism and social climbing, is unattainable and destructive.

Regarding the priority question: The primary use of a bed is for sleeping.
